article.body:
Persistent internal states function as operational memory only when they provide predictive sufficiency, meaning a system's current state allows it to make useful predictions about its own future [1, 2, 4]. We are finding that there is an inevitable trade-off here; simplifying a system to model it, much like zooming out on a map until only the major highways remain, limits the detail you can capture [1, 4]. This means that maintaining a reliable record is not free; it demands a constant, often significant, expenditure of energy to combat the natural tendency of systems to lose information over time [5, 6]. Our work continues to refine the mathematical bounds on these energy costs [7, 8].

Beyond just storing a memory internally, we are examining how information becomes objective, meaning different independent observers can agree on what the record says [10, 11, 14]. This process typically involves redundancy, where a system proliferates copies of its internal state into its surrounding environment [12, 14]. Think of this like a person in a crowded room shouting the same fact repeatedly; even if a listener was initially distracted, the sheer volume of identical signals makes the information hard to miss [12]. While this broadcasting makes records robust, it faces a natural adversary [13]. If the environment scrambles information too quickly, it can effectively erase those copies, creating a constant tension between the system's need to broadcast its history and the environment's tendency to shuffle the data [13].

Our research also extends into chemical networks that sustain themselves through self-reinforcing loops, known as autocatalytic networks [15, 16, 17]. These systems rely on specific recipes of ingredients, described technically as stoichiometric conditions, to keep their cycles running [15, 17, 18]. We are now exploring whether simply keeping a reaction cycle going counts as a meaningful memory, or if there is a specific, as-yet-unclear threshold where these persistent compositions transition into true heredity [17, 18]. Determining this distinction matters because it separates simple non-equilibrium persistence from the building blocks of biological evolution [16, 18].

If these chemical networks can store reliable history, how do they preserve that information against the disruptive noise of a flow reactor, and at what point does copying fidelity become high enough to support actual adaptation rather than just repetition?

Summary

Our group is studying how physical systems keep records of their past. We are learning that storing information is costly and that simplifying a model usually reduces the accuracy of what we can remember. We also found that records become objective when systems broadcast their states into the environment, creating multiple copies that observers can verify. Finally, we are looking at chemical networks to see when a self-sustaining reaction cycle changes from merely repeating itself into a system capable of passing on its history. We still do not know exactly when this shift to heredity happens.
article.lede: We are investigating how physical systems reliably store their own history, how that information becomes accessible to independent observers, and the exact threshold where chemical cycles begin to act like evolving lineages.
article.lens: This progress update synthesizes research on the physical limits of causal memory, the mechanisms of objective record-keeping via environmental redundancy, and the stoichiometric constraints governing chemical self-persistence.
article.title: Persistent Records, Public Reliability, and Chemical Lineages
